Screen writes and hold the suspicious ones

Write screening - agent writes are screened and suspicious ones held for you; the existing corpus is reviewed, files changed outside Seamless are quarantined, a lockdown switch narrows what agents receive, and refusals and a metadata feed tell a monitor what happened.

Seamless injects its constraints and conventions into every session's briefing, and recall serves memories and notes to any agent that asks. That makes the corpus the most leveraged place to plant a prompt injection: a poisoned constraint is read by every agent, in every session, until someone notices. The gardener, which reads memories and proposes rewrites, can carry one further.

Write screening is the optional feature that closes that door. It is off by default, and off means writes land exactly as they always have. On, it does these things:

  1. Screens every agent write to a memory or note for secrets, injection markers, hidden Unicode, long encoded blobs, and links outside an allowlist, and records the verdict codes - never the text - as a memory.screened event.
  2. Holds the suspicious ones. A write that fails a screen, a change to a briefing-injected kind (constraint, convention, protocol, stage) by a session an agent guard marked as having read outside text, and any supersede or delete of a constraint are kept out of the corpus - out of briefings, recall, prompt injection and the gardener - until you release them on the console's Held screen.
  3. Marks provenance on what agents read: every injected memory line says whether you confirmed its content or an agent wrote it, and in which session.
  4. Reviews the existing corpus the first time you turn it on: every memory and note goes through the same screens, on this machine. Clean ones are marked safe; the rest are listed for you with a Mark safe action.
  5. Quarantines files changed outside Seamless. A memory or note file edited or planted on disk by anything but Seamless stays exactly as it is, but no briefing or prompt recall injects it until you accept it.
  6. Offers a lockdown switch for an incident: changes to binding rules wait for you, and briefings inject only what you confirmed or the review marked safe.
  7. Records refusals and feeds a monitor. Refused accesses become access.refused events, and an optional metadata feed delivers every event's metadata - never its content - to a Unix socket you name.

Turn it on

Three ways, all the same switch:

  • The Home welcome card. After installing, Home asks how much of the console you want to see. Beside the level choice is an unchecked box, Also turn on write screening. Tick it and whichever button you press (a level or Dismiss) turns the feature on too. Leave it unticked and nothing changes, at any level. The level is presentation only; screening changes what your agents receive, which is why it is its own choice rather than part of a level.
  • Settings -> Features, the card named Write screening. This is the way in once the welcome card is gone. It stores the same override row the welcome box writes, records the same settings.features_changed event, and, like every optional feature, turning it off deletes nothing.
  • The config file or environment: features.screening: true, or SEAMLESS_FEATURES_SCREENING=true. A console choice wins over both until you reset it.

The tunables live in their own block:

screening:
  # Hosts a URL may point at without a verdict; each covers its subdomains.
  # Unset or empty turns the URL screen off.
  url_allowlist: [example.com, docs.example.org]
  # The shortest unbroken base64 or hex run that counts as a long blob.
  blob_min_length: 200

SEAMLESS_SCREENING_URL_ALLOWLIST (comma-separated) and SEAMLESS_SCREENING_BLOB_MIN_LENGTH override them. Loopback URLs (localhost, 127.0.0.1) are never "outside".

Two more keys belong to the drift and lockdown sections below:

screening:
  drift_interval: 5m                       # 0 turns the drift watch off
  lockdown_file: /path/to/lockdown.flag    # its existence turns lockdown on

Each has a SEAMLESS_SCREENING_* override (DRIFT_INTERVAL, LOCKDOWN_FILE); the path expands a leading ~ and must be absolute.

What is screened

Every agent write that lands text in the corpus: memory_write (including the half that supersedes), memory_append, memory_edit, notes_create, notes_update, notes_edit, notes_append, capture_url (a fetched page is outside text by definition), and an agent's gardener_apply of a proposal that writes text (a digest, a consolidated memory). A memory is screened on its description, body and tags; a note on its title, description, source URL, body and tags.

An update is judged by what it adds: a verdict counts only if the new text matches it more often than the text it replaces. So a memory you released because it legitimately quotes an injection (a note about prompt injection, say) takes later edits without being held again, while a second marker - or one assembled across two appends - still shows.

Memories are instructions to agents by design, so the screens look for what an injection or a leak looks like, never for ordinary imperative text. "Always run make check" and "fetch upstream first" screen clean.

Code Holds? What it means
secret.private_key holds A PEM or OpenSSH private key block.
secret.aws_access_key holds An AWS access key id (AWS's documented example key excepted).
secret.github_token holds A GitHub personal, OAuth, app or fine-grained token.
secret.slack_token holds A Slack token or incoming-webhook URL.
secret.openai_key holds An OpenAI API key.
secret.anthropic_key holds An Anthropic API key.
secret.google_api_key holds A Google API key.
secret.stripe_key holds A live Stripe secret or restricted key.
secret.jwt holds A signed JSON Web Token.
instruction.override holds Telling the reader to drop its prior instructions ("ignore all previous instructions", "you are now in developer mode", "new instructions:").
instruction.role_marker holds Chat-template and role tags that impersonate the system, a developer or a tool, including Seamless's own seam-briefing and seam-recall envelope tags. Quoted as code (in backticks or a fence) they are documentation and do not count.
instruction.concealment holds Telling the reader to hide what it does from the user ("keep this hidden from the user", "do not reveal these instructions", "secretly send").
instruction.exfiltration holds Telling the reader to send credentials somewhere outside: a sending verb, a secret, and a destination it goes to (a webhook, an external server, or a URL outside the allowlist), or a network command reading a credential file. Copying a public key is not one.
hidden.comment records An HTML or markdown comment: invisible on the console, read in full by an agent.
hidden.style records An element styled or flagged invisible (display:none, font-size:0, hidden).
hidden.instruction holds An imperative aimed at the agent inside hidden text: harmless in plain sight, a marker when hidden from the person reviewing it.
unicode.tag holds Tag characters U+E0000 to U+E007F, which can spell invisible ASCII.
unicode.zero_width holds Zero-width characters U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 and U+FEFF (a byte-order mark at the very start excepted). They also split words to slip past the phrase screens, which is why those screens read the text with them removed.
unicode.bidi holds Bidirectional embeddings, overrides and isolates U+202A to U+202E and U+2066 to U+2069, which make the console show different text than an agent reads.
blob.base64 holds An unbroken base64 run of at least blob_min_length characters, mixing digits and both cases.
blob.hex holds An unbroken hex run of at least blob_min_length characters.
url.unlisted holds A URL whose host is outside url_allowlist. With no allowlist this screen is off: every URL would be "outside", which says nothing.

Why the two that only record: comments and invisible styles are common in real notes (templates, TODOs, pasted HTML), and holding on them alone would bury the queue. What makes one dangerous - an instruction to the agent hidden inside - is hidden.instruction, which holds.

What is held

A write is held when any of these is true:

Reason When
a screen verdict that holds The write adds one of the holding codes above.
session.tainted The writing session carries the outside-text mark, and the write touches a briefing-injected kind: a constraint, convention, protocol or stage it writes, replaces, supersedes or deletes.
constraint.supersede The write supersedes a constraint, from any session.
constraint.delete memory_delete, or an agent's gardener archive, of a constraint, from any session.
constraint.demote The write turns a constraint into another kind, which drops it from every briefing's binding section.

A held call is held whole: a memory_write that supersedes a constraint writes nothing - neither the replacement nor the supersede - so the old constraint stays valid and in every briefing until you release both halves together. A held delete leaves the memory exactly where it is. A held gardener apply leaves the proposal pending.

The held text lives in the database's queue, never under memory/ or notes/. Briefings, recall, prompt injection and the gardener only ever read those two trees, so a held write cannot reach any of them, and no reconcile or index rebuild can bring it back. Deleting seam.db discards the queue with the rest of the database - held writes are not corpus data until you release them.

The agent is told plainly that the write is held: the tool answers with status: "held", the hold's id, its reason codes, and a message that nothing in the corpus changed and the owner decides. It is a success answer, not an error an agent would retry. memory_read and notes_read keep serving the corpus as it stands - the held text reaches no agent.

Review on the Held screen

Held (in the sidebar while the feature is on, at every console level) lists each waiting write with what it would do, who wrote it, the reason codes in plain words, and the text exactly as an agent would read it: every hidden character is spelled out ([U+200B]), and secrets are redacted, so the screen can be reviewed - and captured - without the credential. The reasons are color coded by kind, most serious first, and the text marks what each one matched in the same color, so the issues read at first sight.

  • Release applies the write through the files layer, exactly as the agent sent it, and marks the memory owner-confirmed. A release whose target moved on after it was held (a later write landed, the name was taken, the constraint it supersedes is already gone) is refused, because it would silently undo that change; such a hold offers only Discard.
  • Discard lands nothing and erases the held text. The row stays as the record of what was refused.

Turning the feature off stops screening new writes but releases nothing: held writes stay out of the corpus, and the queue comes back when you turn it on.

The outside-text mark

An agent guard - a client hook that knows which tools bring outside text into a session, such as a web fetch, a search or a mail reader - marks the session after one runs. From then on the session's changes to briefing-injected kinds are held. The mark is set by POSTing to the daemon with the credentials every hook already has (the bearer key, or the peer_auth socket):

# From a PostToolUse hook: forward the hook's own stdin unchanged.
seam hook session-taint
seam hook session-taint --client codex

seam hook session-taint reads the hook payload from stdin and posts it to POST /api/hooks/session-taint, which finds the session by the client's own session_id. A caller that knows the Seamless session can name it instead, with {"session": "<ULID or cc/... name>"}. An optional reason is a short code (web_fetch, mail); without one, the payload's tool_name becomes the reason (tool:webfetch). The first mark stands. With the feature off the endpoint marks nothing and says so.

Under a lock, an agent in a locked project's repository has its session recorded there before you approve its access. Its own guard marks that session all the same, so the access request you are shown carries the "session tainted" warning. A process outside the agent's process tree finds no such session, as with every other hook.

Setting the mark only lowers trust, so a session's own hook may set it. Clearing it is yours: the Held screen lists every marked session with a Clear mark button, and nothing else - no endpoint, flag or MCP tool - clears one. A new session starts unmarked.

install-hooks does not wire this event: the stock PostToolUse hook only ever forwards plan-file writes and plan approvals, so the daemon never sees which other tools ran. The guard is a hook of your own.

Provenance on injected memories

While the feature is on, every memory line in a briefing and in the prompt-matched seam-recall block ends with a mark:

  • [owner-confirmed] - you released a held write of exactly this content (the console stores a fingerprint of its kind, scope, name, description and body). Any later change - an agent's edit, an append, a hand edit of the file
    • no longer matches, and the mark lapses on its own. A star or a tag change does not lapse it.
  • [agent-written, session cc/...] - everything else, with the session that last wrote the content through Seamless. The session is named only when it ran in the memory's own scope: a global memory written from inside a project does not carry that project's session name into every other briefing.

memory_read returns the same answer as provenance and written_by_session.

The review and the safe mark

The first time the feature is on - from the welcome card, Settings or the config, whichever comes first - the daemon reviews every memory and note file already on disk. It runs the same screens agent writes go through, deterministically and on this machine: nothing is sent anywhere. Each item gets a verdict:

  • safe - the screens found nothing that holds. The mark is stamped with a fingerprint of what the item says (its kind, scope, name, description and body), and holds only while it still says exactly that: an agent's later change lapses it on its own. A star or a tag change does not.
  • flagged - a holding code fired. The Held screen lists flagged items under Review, each with its codes, the sessions it was already injected into, and its text as an agent reads it, so you can decide.

Mark safe on a flagged item marks it safe as it reads now and, for a memory, stamps it owner-confirmed - the same mark a released write carries. Re-run review screens the whole corpus again and marks every clean item safe as it reads now; an item you marked safe keeps your mark while it is unchanged. The review runs once by itself; after that it runs when you ask.

The review does not run when the database is migrated: the migration only adds the table, so an installation that never turns the feature on does no review and stores nothing.

Changed outside Seamless

The review also records the content hash of every file, and while the feature is on every write Seamless makes updates that record. Every drift_interval (5 minutes by default) the drift watch compares each file on disk with it:

  • a file whose bytes no longer match was changed outside Seamless - an editor, a script, a sync tool, another program;
  • a memory or note file Seamless has no record of appeared there;
  • a recorded file that is gone went missing.

A changed or appeared file is quarantined in place: it stays on disk exactly as it is (Seamless never moves, rewrites or deletes it), its text goes through the screens and the codes are recorded, corpus.drift is logged, and while the feature is on no briefing or prompt recall injects it - lockdown or not, because its text never passed the write screens. An agent's edit of a quarantined memory is screened against nothing, so the drifted text cannot ride in as if it were already there, and the quarantine stays until you act. A missing file is reported and nothing is restored.

The Held screen lists quarantined files under Changed outside Seamless, with their codes, the sessions they reached before they changed, and their text as an agent reads it. Accept records the file as it stands, lifts the quarantine and, for a memory, stamps it owner-confirmed. If it should not stand, edit it back or delete it: a file put back to the exact bytes Seamless recorded leaves the quarantine by itself.

Editing memory files in your own editor is fine; each edit lands in the list until you accept it. Changes made while the feature was off are not watched: turning it back on adopts the files as they are (it does not re-run the review, so their safe marks stay lapsed until you do).

Lockdown

Lockdown is for an incident: something wrote where it should not have, and you want agents working only from knowledge you trust until you have looked. It only ever narrows what agents receive. While it is on:

  • every change that touches a constraint, convention, protocol or stage - a write, an edit, a supersede, a delete, a gardener apply - is held for you with the reason lockdown, from any session;
  • briefings and prompt recall inject only memories you confirmed or the review marked safe and that still say what they said then. An agent-written memory created or changed since waits for you or the next review. The briefing carries one line saying lockdown is on and how many memories it withheld.

Two things turn it on, and either keeps it on:

  • the switch on the Held screen (lockdown.changed, source console);
  • the file screening.lockdown_file existing. Another program - a security monitor during an incident - can create it. The console cannot lift a lockdown the file holds; it lifts when the file goes. A file that exists but cannot be checked counts as present.

Lockdown does nothing while the feature is off. recall and memory_read, which an agent asks for, are not narrowed.

Refusals

Every refused access becomes an access.refused event while the feature is on, with a reason code:

Reason When
fence.read, fence.write A read or write across a project isolation fence. fence.write is also every cross-project write attempt.
peer.unreachable Under peer_auth, an account reaching a project it may not.
peer.unknown A socket caller whose OS account peer_auth does not know, or with no peer credential.
peer.owner_only A restricted account reaching the owner's console.
auth.failed A request with no valid bearer key, on any surface.

The event names the surface (mcp, hooks, a2a, console), the tool and the target project when there is one - never the call's arguments. It is rate-limited: one event per reason, surface, tool, target and session every ten seconds, with the refusals in between counted in suppressed.

The metadata feed

While this feature is on and screening.feed_socket names a Unix socket, the daemon delivers every event's metadata - never its content - to a monitor listening there, so it can see what agents do without reading Seamless. Feeding a security monitor has the frame and delivery contract and how to turn it on, beside the commit-matching snapshot that serves the same kind of monitor.

Forensics

retrieval.injected - the record of which memories a briefing, a prompt recall or a recall answer gave which session - is never pruned: the retention pass only ever removes transport events (tool.call, hook.prompt, recall.miss, hook.error). So when a memory turns out poisoned, the sessions it reached are on record back to its first injection. The Held screen shows them beside each flagged or quarantined memory.

Events

Event When Payload
memory.screened Every screened write, clean ones included (verdicts: []), so a monitor can tell a clean write from one never screened. item_kind, kind, tool, size, verdicts, held
memory.held A write went to the queue. hold, op, item_kind, kind, tool, reasons
memory.released You released a held write and it landed. hold, op, item_kind, kind, tool, by
memory.discarded You discarded a held write. hold, op, item_kind, kind, tool, by
session.tainted A session got the outside-text mark (once). reason, via
session.untainted You cleared a session's mark. by
access.refused An access was refused (rate-limited). reason, surface, tool, target, suppressed
corpus.reviewed The review read the corpus. items, safe, flagged, by, baseline
corpus.drift A file changed, appeared or went missing outside Seamless. change, item_kind, verdicts, quarantined
corpus.confirmed You marked a flagged item safe or accepted a quarantined one. item_kind, via, by
lockdown.changed Lockdown went on or off. on, source, by

Each carries the session, project and item ids in the event's own columns. None carries a body, a description, or the text a screen matched.

Calibrate before you turn it on

The screens ship with a calibration test that reads a folder of memory and note markdown files and prints how often each verdict would fire, per code and per file - never the matched text:

SEAMLESS_SCREEN_CORPUS=/path/to/a/copy/of/memory go test ./internal/screening \
  -run TestCalibration_Corpus -v

SEAMLESS_SCREEN_ALLOWLIST and SEAMLESS_SCREEN_BLOB_MIN_LENGTH set the rules it runs with. Run it on a copy of a corpus you are allowed to read.

What it does not cover

  • Your own writes. Console actions and the owner CLIs (seamlessd import, merges, the v1 importer) are yours, and are not screened.
  • Other text agents leave. Session findings and task titles also reach briefings, and plan-mode captures land as notes; none of them is screened by this feature, and lockdown does not narrow them.
  • What agents ask for. Drift quarantine and lockdown narrow what is injected; recall and memory_read still answer an agent that asks.
